title: Sell Mineral Rights in Baldwin County, AL
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Baldwin County, AL
metaDescription: Own oil and gas interests in Baldwin County, Alabama? Get a hedged, activity-based offer for minerals near Bay Minette, Daphne, Foley, or Elberta.
heroLead: Baldwin County minerals sit on the quiet eastern edge of the Smackover-Norphlet fairway, and most of the parcels we review here trace back to a single family purchase generations ago.
intro: Baldwin County is the largest county in Alabama by land area, and its mineral history is really two overlapping stories. Along the Mobile Bay shoreline and the interior pine flats near Bay Minette and Robertsdale, shallow gas and salt-dome structure extend eastward from the Mobile County core. Farther east and south, toward Foley and Elberta, oil and gas interest was leased more speculatively during the mid-century boom years and rarely developed, which is exactly why so many owners here still hold minerals they've never heard a word about since.

We work with families and individual owners across Baldwin County who inherited a fractional interest, found an old lease in a courthouse abstract, or simply want to convert a line item on a property tax bill into cash. This page walks through how minerals in Baldwin County are typically valued, what ownership tends to look like, and the questions we're asked most before a sale.

sections.heading: Where Baldwin County sits in the play
paragraphs: Baldwin County borders the Mobile Bay side of the Norphlet and Smackover trend that produced the Citronelle Field in neighboring Mobile County and Jay Field along the Alabama-Florida line to the east. The county itself has seen far less drilling than either neighbor, but the same salt-dome and reef-trend geology underlies much of the western and southern county, which is why leasing activity has periodically picked up along the bay and near the Escambia County line without ever turning into sustained production for most tracts.

That history matters for value. A Baldwin County interest with no producing well nearby is priced very differently than one sitting inside an active drilling or spacing unit, and offers here are appropriately centered on lease-bonus comparables and permit activity rather than a royalty check history, since most owners in the county have never received one.

sections.heading: How ownership usually looks here
paragraphs: Baldwin County's rapid growth along the Highway 59 and coastal corridors has pushed a lot of surface land into subdivisions, but mineral rights were commonly severed decades before that development and never followed the surface sale. It's routine for us to see a 40 or 80-acre mineral tract, sometimes reserved by a grandparent or great-grandparent who sold the surface but kept the minerals, now divided among a dozen or more heirs who may not even know the interest exists.

Because Baldwin County's probate court in Bay Minette handles the wills, estate filings, and heir determinations for property across the county, a title search there is usually the fastest way to confirm exactly who owns what percentage before any offer is finalized. If a prior owner died without a will, Alabama's intestate succession rules typically split the interest among children or, absent children, other next of kin, which is where tenancy-in-common ownership among cousins often originates.

sections.heading: Split estate and non-participating interests
paragraphs: A meaningful share of the Baldwin County parcels we look at are split estate, meaning the surface belongs to one owner (often a developer, farm, or timber operation today) while the mineral estate was reserved separately, sometimes generations ago. Others are non-participating royalty interests, where the owner is entitled to a royalty share if production ever occurs but has no right to sign a lease or negotiate bonus terms themselves.

Both situations are sellable, but the mechanics differ. A non-participating royalty interest is generally valued on a narrower set of comparables than a full mineral interest with executive rights, and we walk owners through which category their deed actually places them in before quoting anything.

sections.heading: What we look at before making an offer
paragraphs: For any Baldwin County tract, we pull the county's current permit and leasing activity, check whether the parcel falls inside or near an established Alabama Oil and Gas Board field order, and review any prior lease history recorded at the courthouse. Interests near the Mobile County line or close to historic Norphlet-Smackover structure tend to carry a different range than interests in the county's eastern interior, where activity has been thinner.

From there we quote a range tied to that activity rather than a flat number, and we're upfront when a specific tract is thinly traded, since an honest range beats a number we can't stand behind six months later.

faqs.question: I inherited part of a mineral interest in Baldwin County but I'm not sure how much. Can you still make an offer?
faqs.answer: Yes. We regularly work from a probate file or an old deed rather than a clean title report. We'll help identify your fractional share as part of the process, and the offer is scaled to whatever percentage you can document.

faqs.question: There's no well on or near my Baldwin County land. Is the interest worth anything?
faqs.answer: It can be, though the range is lower than for a producing tract and depends heavily on nearby permit activity and how close the parcel sits to the Norphlet-Smackover trend. We'll tell you plainly if current activity doesn't support much of an offer.

faqs.question: My mineral interest is non-participating royalty, not a full mineral estate. Does that change anything?
faqs.answer: It changes the valuation approach, not whether we can buy it. A non-participating royalty interest is priced on a different set of comparables since you don't hold executive rights, but it's still a sellable asset.

faqs.question: Do I need to hire an attorney before selling minerals in Baldwin County?
faqs.answer: We're not attorneys and can't give legal advice, and for a straightforward inherited fractional interest most owners don't need one for the transaction itself. For complicated estates, unresolved probate, or disputes among heirs, talking to a local real estate or estate attorney first is worth the cost.

faqs.question: How long does closing usually take on a Baldwin County mineral sale?
faqs.answer: Once ownership and acreage are confirmed against the county's records, most straightforward sales close within a few weeks. Estates still in active probate or interests split among many unlocated heirs take longer, since every owner's share has to be documented before closing.
